title: Module 10: Timber design to EC5
whyItMatters: Timber is heavily used in both UK residential/refurbishment permanent works (floor joists, rafters, lintels, engineered glulam/LVL) and site temporary works (soleboards, bearers, walings, hoardings), and behaves very differently from isotropic steel.
introduction: Covers solid softwood/hardwood and engineered timber products (glulam, LVL, CLT), strength classes (e.g. C16, C24, GL24h), orthotropic grain direction dependence, moisture Service Classes (1, 2, and 3), load-duration classes and modification factor k_mod, design strength f_d = k_mod · f_k / γ_M, bending, shear, bearing perpendicular to grain, tension perpendicular to grain (splitting at notches and holes), lateral restraint, creep deformation factor k_def, connections, durability, and char-rate fire awareness.
objectives: Explain why timber is anisotropic and how moisture Service Class and load duration modify design strength via k_mod and long-term deflection via k_def.
Design and check a simple timber floor joist or lintel for bending, shear, deflection, and bearing perpendicular to the grain (Projects 10.1 and 10.2).
Identify why bottom-face notches near supports and holes/connections inducing tension perpendicular to the grain can trigger sudden brittle splitting.
learningGate: Explain physically why timber is not isotropic and how parallel vs perpendicular to grain properties differ.,Explain why bearing compression perpendicular to the grain at supports matters and often governs.,Explain why notches (especially on the tension side near supports) can critically reduce shear capacity.,Explain why moisture content (Service Class) and load duration affect both design strength (k_mod) and long-term deflection (k_def).,Set out the complete check sequence for a simple timber member.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate EC5 design bending strength f_m,d using k_mod and γ_M
